## Synthesis: research report

**Question:** 설계 중인 "기계공학 계산/수치 검증 하니스" 스킬에 들어갈 공학적 내용이 정확한지(잘못된 정보가 없는지) 검증한다. 구체적으로: (1) 제안한 검증 게이트 체계(단위·차원해석, 식 선택 적합성, 입력값 타당성, order-of-magnitude, 안전계수/마진, 가정 노출, 독립 재계산)가 실제 기계공학 계산 검증/V&V 모범사례와 일치하는가 (2) 스킬 치트시트에 들어갈 핵심 공식들의 정확성 — 재료역학(굽힘응력 σ=Mc/I, 처짐, 좌굴 오일러식, 비틀림 τ=Tr/J, 안전계수 정의), 기계요소(볼트 체결 토크 T=KDF, 용접·기어·베어링 수명 L10, 스프링 k), 열전달(전도 푸리에, 대류, 복사), 유체(압력손실 Darcy-Weisbach, 레이놀즈수, 베르누이) (3) 전형적 재질 물성 범위와 안전계수 관례(연성/취성, 정적/피로, 산업별)가 흔히 인용되는 값과 맞는가 (4) 흔한 계산 오류·red flag 목록이 타당한가. 각 항목에 대해 표준 교과서(Shigley, Hibbeler, Norton 등)·핸드북·공인 출처 기준으로 옳음/틀림/주의를 판정하고, 틀리기 쉬운 부분을 지적하라.

25 claims survived 3-vote adversarial verification. Merge semantic duplicates and synthesize.

## Confirmed claims
### [0] ASME defines verification as determining whether the computational model fits the mathematical description (math is solved right), and validation as determining whether the model accurately represents the real-world application (right math/physics) — the two are distinct activities.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/verification-validation-uncertainty (primary)
Quote: "Verification is performed to determine if the computational model fits the mathematical description."
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is verbatim-supported by the primary source. WebFetch of the ASME primary page (asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/verification-validation-uncertainty) returns both halves: "Verification is performed to determine if the computational model fits the mathematical description" AND "Validation is implemented to determine if the model accurately represents the real world application." Independent corroboration: AIAA G-077 ("Verification is the process of determining that a model implementation accurately represents the developer's conceptual description...the solution to the model" vs. "Validation is the process of determining the degree to which a model is an accurate representation of the real world from the perspective of the intended uses"), ASME V&V 10-2019 (verification = "numerical fidelity of the simulation"; validation = "representation of the physics"), and LANL LA-14167-MS. The "solving the equations right" vs. "solving the right equations" gloss is the canonical Roache/AIAA shorthand and matches the claim's paraphrase. The two are explicitly distinct activities in all sources. Terminology stable since AIAA 1998 guide through ASME V&V 10-2019, so not outdated; definitional standards-body statement, not marketing. Only minor nuance (not a refutation): verification is formally split into code verification + solution verification; the one-line claim simplifies this but is not wrong.

### [1] Validation is a separate gate from verification, concerned with real-world fidelity rather than mathematical/numerical correctness.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/verification-validation-uncertainty (primary)
Quote: "Validation is implemented to determine if the model accurately represents the real world application."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is well-supported by the quote and corroborated by multiple independent authoritative sources. The ASME VVUQ primary page (fetched) states verification "is performed to determine if the computational model fits the mathematical description" while validation "is implemented to determine if the model accurately represents the real world application" — exactly the verification (math/numerical correctness) vs. validation (real-world fidelity) split the claim asserts, and confirming they are treated as distinct activities/gates. This is consensus terminology, not an extraordinary claim: the LA-14167-MS Los Alamos report and ASME V&V 10 (computational solid mechanics) / V&V 20 standards define validation as "the degree to which a model is an accurate representation of the real world from the perspective of the intended uses of the model," and verification as determining that the implementation "accurately represents the developer's conceptual description." Echoes the classic Roache/AIAA G-077 distinction: verification = "solving the equations right," validation = "solving the right equations." No credible source disputes or heavily qualifies this; it is current and unchanged across ASME/NAFEMS/AIAA/DOE. The word "gate" is the claim author's framing (V&V are sequential activities — verification logically precedes validation since validating an unverified code is meaningless), but treating them as separate checks is accurate. Minor nuance worth noting for the skill: for a hand-calculation harness (not computational simulation), full ASME-style "validation" against experiment is often out of scope; the claim's distinction is correct but the skill should not overstate that a hand-calc check constitutes formal validation.

### [2] ASME treats V&V plus UQ as the recognized procedural backbone for establishing confidence in computational/engineering models, validating that a multi-gate verification scheme is consistent with established best practice.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.asme.org/codes-standards/publications-information/verification-validation-uncertainty (primary)
Quote: "Assuring that the computational model has been formed using sound procedures is key and is achieved through the processes of verification, validation and uncertainty quantification."
Verifier evidence (high): The core factual claim is well-supported by the primary source (asme.org VVUQ page) and corroborated independently. The supporting quote is verbatim accurate: "Assuring that the computational model has been formed using sound procedures is key and is achieved through the processes of verification, validation and uncertainty quantification (VVUQ)." ASME's claim to V&V/UQ authority is backed by real, established, currently-maintained standards: ASME V&V 10 (Computational Solid Mechanics, first ed. 2006), V&V 20 (CFD & Heat Transfer), and V&V 40-2018 (Credibility of Computational Modeling, Medical Devices). The source is the standards-issuing body itself (primary, authoritative), matching the claim's strength. Independent corroboration: Machine Design article "Standardizing Computational Models: Verification, Validation and Uncertainty Quantification" and FDA/regulatory use of V&V 40 for medical-device in-silico models. Not outdated, not marketing fluff, not forum speculation.

CAVEAT (a partial overreach, not enough to refute): ASME V&V/UQ is scoped to COMPUTATIONAL/simulation models (FEA, CFD), NOT to manual engineering hand-calculations. The claim's tail — "validating that a multi-gate verification scheme is consistent with established best practice" — is an inferential bridge: ASME V&V endorses verification+validation+UQ as a credibility backbone, which is directionally consistent with a multi-gate hand-calc verification scheme (independent recalculation, assumption exposure, uncertainty/margin), but ASME does NOT specifically prescribe the 7-gate hand-calc scheme described in the research question. The principle (sound, documented, multi-step verification establishes confidence) generalizes; the specific gates do not derive from ASME. The claim is true as stated about ASME's stance and the general consistency, so it stands.

### [3] ASME V&V 10-2006 establishes as a core principle that verification must precede validation, where verification is the domain of mathematics and validation is the domain of physics.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/bitstreams/a45e16f4-5cce-44f4-b2bd-fa760019c8aa/download (primary)
Quote: "Verification must precede validation. ... Put most simply, verification is the domain of mathematics and validation is the domain of physics."
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is well-supported and uncontested. WebSearch indexing the exact primary source (NCSU repository PDF, "An Overview of the ASME V&V-10 Guide") confirms both clauses: (1) "One of the key principles laid out in the first V&V standard is that verification must precede validation. The logic is that attempting to validate a model using a code that may still contain (serious) errors can lead to a false conclusion." (2) "Verification is the domain of mathematics and validation is the domain of physics." A second independent overview (Ansys/LS-DYNA "An Overview of the ASME Guide for Verification and Validation") corroborates the same standard. The framing is consistent with the broader V&V canon — Roache: "verification is a mathematics... issue; not a physics issue. Validation is a physical sciences... issue" (Oberkampf/Roy 2010; Roache 1998). ASME V&V 10-2006 (Guide for Verification and Validation in Computational Solid Mechanics) is a real published standard (ISBN 9780791830420), so not outdated and not a marketing claim. The claim faithfully restates the quote without overreach. Minor caveat (not refuting): the "math/physics domain" split is a memorable simplification — validation also relies on statistics/UQ (mathematics) — but it is a faithful reproduction of how the guide itself frames the distinction. Limitation: the primary PDF is compressed and could not be fully text-extracted via WebFetch, so confirmation rests on the search index of that source plus independent secondary corroboration.

### [4] The ASME Guide defines verification as two distinct parts: code verification (removing programming/logic errors so the math model and algorithms work correctly) and calculation verification (estimating numerical errors from discretization).
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/bitstreams/a45e16f4-5cce-44f4-b2bd-fa760019c8aa/download (primary)
Quote: "Code Verification – establish confidence ... that the mathematical model and solution algorithms are working correctly. ... Calculation Verification - establish confidence ... that the discrete solution of the mathematical model is accurate."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim accurately reflects standard ASME V&V-10 doctrine and is directly supported by its quote. Independent corroboration (NCSU "Overview of the ASME V&V-10 Guide" plus ASME/NAFEMS V&V literature) confirms verification is split into two parts: (1) code verification — removing programming/logic/algorithm errors so the mathematical model and solution algorithms work correctly, and (2) calculation verification — estimating numerical errors arising from discretization, performed after code verification so the two error sources are not confounded ("Code verification addresses programming and logic errors...calculation verification estimates the numerical errors due to discretization approximations"). The supporting quote ("mathematical model and solution algorithms are working correctly" / "discrete solution of the mathematical model is accurate") matches the claim without overreach. The framing is consistent with the underlying Roache / Oberkampf & Roy V&V framework. Minor non-refuting caveat: ASME also calls "calculation verification" by the synonym "solution verification," and code verification typically also includes order-of-accuracy/MMS checks beyond pure "logic errors" — but neither contradicts the claim. Source quality (peer-reviewed/academic overview of the actual standard) matches the descriptive, non-extraordinary nature of the claim; no contradicting source found. Could not extract the primary PDF text directly (compressed streams) and the ASME Digital Collection article is paywalled (HTTP 403), so confidence is high but not maximal.

### [5] Validation of a complex system should proceed hierarchically from the component level to the system level, and validation is specific to a particular computational model for a particular intended use.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://repository.lib.ncsu.edu/bitstreams/a45e16f4-5cce-44f4-b2bd-fa760019c8aa/download (primary)
Quote: "Validation of a complex system should be pursued in a hierarchical fashion from the component level to the system level. ... Validation is specific to a particular computational model for a particular intended use."
Verifier evidence (high): The claim is well-supported, current, and consensus V&V methodology — both halves are verifiable against primary/standard sources, not just the cited NCSU repository PDF.

PART 1 ("hierarchical, component→system level"): Matches ASME V&V 10-2006 (Standard for Verification and Validation in Computational Solid Mechanics) almost verbatim: "Validation of a complex system should be pursued in a hierarchical fashion from the component level to the system level," with the system decomposed into assemblies/subassemblies/components. This is also the canonical "validation hierarchy / validation pyramid" of Oberkampf & Roy (foundational CFD/CSM V&V work), reaffirmed in current literature (e.g., ScienceDirect "Model validation hierarchies for connecting system design to modeling and simulation," 2023; NASA NTRS "Exploitation of a Validation Hierarchy," 2023; Frontiers Nuclear Eng. 2025). Standard guidance also notes the complement: system-level V&V is still needed to capture nonlinear interactions a bottom-up approach may miss — consistent with, not contradicting, the claim.

PART 2 ("validation is specific to a particular model for a particular intended use"): A textbook V&V tenet. ASME V&V 10 and Oberkampf/Roy state validation requirements and accuracy tolerances are dictated by the model's intended use; validation assesses whether the quantity of interest is within an intended-use-determined tolerance of the prediction. National Academies VVUQ report and AIAA guidelines echo this.

Checklist results: (1) quote fully supports claim, no overreach; (2) WebSearch found corroboration across ASME, NASA, AIAA, National Academies, peer-reviewed journals — no contradicting source; (3) source quality adequate — claim traces to a published consensus ASME standard and widely cited Oberkampf work, exceeding what a non-extraordinary methodological claim requires; (4) not outdated — concept dates to early-2000s CFD V&V and is reaffirmed in 2023-2025 publications; (5) not marketing.

Minor caveat (does not refute): the claim is a normative best-practice ("should"), not a universal law — pure bottom-up component validation is recognized as insufficient without system-level confirmation, and a strict component-to-system hierarchy is not always feasible for tightly coupled multi-physics systems. But the claim as worded matches standard guidance.

### [6] ASME V&V 20 separates verification into 'code verification' (establishes the code correctly solves the mathematical model, i.e. is free of mistakes) and 'solution/calculation verification' (estimates numerical accuracy of a particular calculation), with code verification preceding validation. This supports a V&V harness gate structure that distinguishes equation-correctness from numerical-accuracy checks and an 'independent re-calculation / equation-correctness' gate.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1368927 (primary)
Quote: "Code verification (V&V-20): "Establishes that the code accurately solves the mathematical model incorporated in the code, i.e. that the code is free of mistakes for the simulations of interest." Solution verification (V&V-20): Estimates the numerical accuracy of a particular calculation."
Verifier evidence (high): The supporting quote is verbatim accurate. Direct text extraction of the OSTI PDF (1368927, "Overview of ASME V&V 20-2009," K. Dowding, Sandia, 2016 Inverse Problems Symposium) reads: "Code verification (V&V-20): 'Establishes that the code accurately solves the mathematical model incorporated in the code, i.e. that the code is free of mistakes for the simulations of interest.' Solution verification (V&V-20): Estimates the numerical accuracy of a particular calculation. Code Verification precedes validation... Goal is finding and removing mistakes in the source code and numerical algorithms. Solution (Calculation) Verification performed as part of validation - Assuring the numerical accuracy of code output." So the claim is faithfully sourced, not an overreach. The underlying doctrine is mainstream and uncontested: code verification (mistake-free code, e.g. Method of Manufactured Solutions) vs solution/calculation verification (numerical/discretization accuracy, e.g. Grid Convergence Index), with verification preceding validation ("solving the equations right" vs "solving the right equations," Roache; Oberkampf & Roy). Multiple sources confirm V&V 20 operationalizes both code verification (MMS) and solution verification (GCI). This correctly supports a harness gate distinguishing equation-correctness from numerical-accuracy and an independent re-calculation gate. CAVEATS (precision, not contradiction): (1) source is a secondary Sandia conference slide deck, not the standard text itself; (2) the code/calculation-verification taxonomy is most canonically associated with the companion standard ASME V&V 10 (Computational Solid Mechanics, 2006) — the same slide even labels the high-level Verification definition "(V&V-10, high level document for solid mechanics)" — so attributing the split specifically to V&V 20 is slightly loose, though defensible since V&V 20 uses the same terms. No credible source contradicts the distinction; it is stable textbook doctrine, not a fast-moving or extraordinary claim, so a secondary overview source is adequate.

### [7] Validation is defined as determining the degree to which a model is an accurate representation of the real world from the perspective of the model's intended uses, framed as a quantitative, possibly iterative process tied to adequacy/intended use. This validates the skill's emphasis on '식 선택 적합성' (fitness of chosen equation for the intended problem) as a recognized V&V gate.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1368927 (primary)
Quote: "Definition Validation (ASME V&V-10/V&V-20): "The process of determining the degree to which a model is an accurate representation of the real world from the perspective of the intended uses of the model.""
Verifier evidence (high): The supporting quote is genuine, accurately reproduced, and correctly attributed. Confirmed via the cited primary source (OSTI 1368927, "Overview of ASME V&V 20-2009") and independent corroboration: ASME V&V-10/V&V-20 define Validation as "The process of determining the degree to which a model is an accurate representation of the real world from the perspective of the intended uses of the model." The "intended uses" clause is integral to the standard's definition and genuinely grounds the principle that a model/equation must be fit for its intended purpose. The core inference — that fitness-for-intended-use is a recognized V&V principle — is therefore defensible and standards-backed.

CAVEAT (framing overreach, not a refutation): In ASME V&V, "validation" specifically means empirical comparison of model predictions against real-world experimental observations (the "comparator") with uncertainty quantification — "validation is the domain of physics," distinct from verification (math/code correctness). The skill's "식 선택 적합성" gate is a pre-computation desk-check of equation appropriateness (e.g., Euler vs. Johnson buckling, thin- vs. thick-wall), which maps more precisely to ASME's notions of conceptual/model-form adequacy and domain of applicability than to the comparator-based validation captured by this single sentence. So the claim slightly conflates equation-selection screening with formal ASME validation. This is a modest imprecision in framing, not a factual error, fabricated quote, contradicted statement, or low-quality source. No credible source disputes the definition; the standard (V&V-10, reaffirmed/updated through 2019) is current. Threshold for refutation not met.

### [8] The validation standard uncertainty combines, assuming independence, numerical solution uncertainty (unum), simulation input uncertainty (uinput), and experimental measurement uncertainty (uD) in quadrature: uval = sqrt(unum^2 + uinput^2 + uD^2). This corroborates that a rigorous engineering-calc verification framework should separately track input-value validity, numerical/model error, and measurement uncertainty as distinct uncertainty sources.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1368927 (primary)
Quote: "unum – uncertainty due to numerical solution of the equations ... uinput – uncertainty due to simulation input uncertainty ... uD – uncertainty due to experimental measurement uncertainty"
Verifier evidence (high): The equation u_val = sqrt(u_num^2 + u_input^2 + u_D^2) is verbatim the ASME V&V 20-2009 standard's validation-uncertainty formulation. Multiple independent sources confirm "u_val² = u_num² + u_input² + u_D²" combining the three components (numerical solution, simulation input, experimental measurement uncertainty) in quadrature, AND confirm the claim's "assuming independence" qualifier is the standard's own stated condition: the quadrature form applies "when the errors are independent," with V&V 20 providing separate methodology when they are not. The supporting quote's definitions of u_num/u_input/u_D match the standard's nomenclature exactly. Source quality is adequate: OSTI 1368927 ("Overview of ASME V&V 20-2009 Standard," authored by the V&V 20 committee) is an authoritative summary of an ASME consensus standard, corroborated by the original Coleman overview paper, NIST IR 8298, and NUREG/CR-7274. The WebFetch of the OSTI PDF failed (scanned/encoded binary, unparseable), but the content was independently corroborated via web search of the standard. Minor soft spot: the framework-generalization sentence conflates V&V 20's statistical "input uncertainty" with "input-value validity" (plausibility checking), and V&V 20 is specifically a CFD/heat-transfer computational-model validation standard rather than a general hand-calc verification standard — but this is a mild scope nuance, not a factual error. The core technical claim (the equation, its three-source decomposition, the independence assumption) is accurate and well-supported.

### [9] The rotary-beam (unmodified) endurance limit for steels is estimated as Se' = 0.5*Sut for Sut up to about 1400 MPa (200 kpsi), with a cap: Se' = 700 MPa (100 kpsi) for steels above that threshold. This is Shigley Eq. (6-10), used repeatedly across solutions.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.secs.oakland.edu/~latcha/ME4300/SM_PDF/CH6.pdf (primary)
Quote: "Eq. (6-10): Se  0.5Sut  0.5(1020)  510 MPa ... Sut > 200 kpsi, Se  100 kpsi ... Sut > 1400 MPa, so Se = 700 MPa"
Verifier evidence (high): Verified by direct pdftotext extraction of the primary source (Shigley's MED 11th ed. Chapter 6 Solutions, secs.oakland.edu — credible academic host). Exact text found: (1) "Eq. (6-10): Se = 0.5Sut = 0.5(1020) = 510 MPa" — confirms Se' = 0.5·Sut labeled Eq. (6-10); (2) "Sut > 200 kpsi, Se = 100 kpsi" (under Eq. 6-10); (3) "Sut > 1400 MPa, so Se = 700 MPa". The label "Eq. (6-10)" appears in dozens of separate problem solutions (lines 3, 12, 20, 26, 36, 127, 225, 288, 367, 455, 629, 804, 944, 1215, 1288...), directly confirming "used repeatedly across solutions." Numbers are standard and cross-confirmed by independent sources (ScienceDirect, sdcverifier). The 0.5 coefficient (vs older 0.504) is the 8th-edition-onward convention, also confirmed. Minor nuance, not a refutation: the piecewise cap is, in Shigley's main TEXT, often the boxed Eq. (6-8); the SOLUTIONS MANUAL labels the whole correlation "Eq. (6-10)." The claim quotes the solutions manual, so its citation is internally consistent. Engineering content and all numeric values (0.5·Sut, 700 MPa/100 kpsi cap, 1400 MPa/200 kpsi threshold) are accurate and current.

### [10] The corrected (Marin) endurance limit is computed as Se = ka*kb*kc*Se' (Eq. 6-17), where ka = a*Sut^b is the surface factor from Table 6-2 (Eq. 6-18), kb = 1.24*d^-0.107 is the size factor for d in mm (Eq. 6-19), and kc = 1 for bending (Eq. 6-25). Example: ka=0.767, kb=0.879, kc=1, Se'=285 -> Se=192 MPa.
Vote: 2-1 · Source: https://www.secs.oakland.edu/~latcha/ME4300/SM_PDF/CH6.pdf (primary)
Quote: "Eq. (6-18): ka  aSubt  3.04(570)0.217  0.767  Eq. (6-19): kb  1.24d 0.107  1.24(25)0.107  0.879  Eq. (6-25): kc  1  Eq. (6-17): Se  kakbkcSe'  (0.767)(0.879)(1)(285)  192 MPa"
Verifier evidence (high): Every element of the claim verified against Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design (10th/11th ed.) conventions and confirmed arithmetically. (1) Equation numbers are correct: Eq. 6-17 (Se = ka*kb*kc*...*Se'), Eq. 6-18 (ka = a*Sut^b, surface factor from Table 6-2), Eq. 6-19 (kb = 1.24*d^-0.107 for d in mm, valid 2.79-51mm), Eq. 6-25 (kc=1 bending, 0.85 axial, 0.59 torsion) all match Shigley. (2) Arithmetic verified: ka = 3.04*570^(-0.217) = 0.767 (a=3.04,b=-0.217 are the cold-drawn-surface Table 6-2 constants in MPa); kb = 1.24*25^(-0.107) = 0.879; Se = 0.767*0.879*1*285 = 192.1 MPa -> 192 MPa. All exact. (3) The supporting quote reproduces every value (0.767, 0.879, 1, 285, 192). (4) Source is Oakland University's hosted Shigley solution manual, a primary-grade source corroborated by independent search results (sciencedirect, engineersedge, multiple university course PDFs) showing the identical Se = ka*kb*kc*kd*ke*kf*Se' formulation. Minor note (not an error): the full Marin Eq. 6-17 has six factors (adds kd temperature, ke reliability, kf misc); the claim's three-factor form is the standard reduced presentation when kd=ke=kf=1, exactly as the cited example does it. A skill cheat-sheet should show the full six-factor form to avoid users forgetting kd/ke/kf, but the claim as a worked example is accurate. No contradicting evidence found.

### [11] For a completely reversed stress state, the fatigue factor of safety is defined as the ratio of the corrected endurance limit to the fully-reversed stress amplitude: nf = Se / sigma_ar.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.secs.oakland.edu/~latcha/ME4300/SM_PDF/CH6.pdf (primary)
Quote: "For completely reversed stress, the fatigue factor of safety can be assessed as the ratio of the endurance limit to the completely reversed stress. nf  Se  ar"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim VERIFIED — not refuted. The supporting quote is reproduced VERBATIM in the primary source. I downloaded and text-extracted the actual PDF (Shigley's Mechanical Engineering Design 11th ed. solutions manual, https://www.secs.oakland.edu/~latcha/ME4300/SM_PDF/CH6.pdf), which states word-for-word: "For completely reversed stress, the fatigue factor of safety can be assessed as the ratio of the endurance limit to the completely reversed stress. nf = Se / σar". The PDF also contains worked numerical examples confirming the formula, e.g. nf = Se/σar = 192/317.8 = 0.60. This is the standard, current, universally-taught definition: for a fully-reversed stress state (R = -1, mean stress σm = 0), the fatigue factor of safety equals the fully-corrected (Marin-modified) endurance limit Se divided by the reversed stress amplitude σa (= σar). Source quality is appropriate — a flagship ME textbook (Budynas & Nisbett / Shigley) used in nearly every mechanical engineering curriculum, and the same definition is corroborated by Norton, BYU ME372 course notes, and ANSYS/durability references found in search. The claim is correctly scoped: it explicitly restricts itself to "completely reversed stress." The only nuance (NOT a refutation) is that when mean stress is nonzero, this simple ratio no longer applies and one must use Goodman/Gerber/ASME-elliptic mean-stress criteria — but the claim does not assert otherwise. No contradicting credible source found; not outdated; not marketing/cherry-picked. For a skill cheatsheet, one wording caution worth flagging: "Se" must denote the CORRECTED endurance limit (after Marin factors ka·kb·kc·kd·ke·kf), not the raw uncorrected Se' = 0.5·Sut — the claim's phrase "corrected endurance limit" handles this correctly.

### [12] Failure to convert non-SI to SI units in software caused the loss of the NASA Mars Climate Orbiter (1998), a $327.6 million failure, demonstrating that unit/dimensional conversion errors produce catastrophic engineering outcomes.
Vote: 3-0 · Source: https://www.nist.gov/pml/owm/metrication-errors-and-mishaps (primary)
Quote: "a subcontractor did not properly account for changing the non-SI measurements in its software"
Verifier evidence (high): Claim is well-supported and accurate. NASA's official mishap investigation (corroborated by Wikipedia citing the MCO Mishap Investigation Board, and the NIST source) confirms: (1) the Mars Climate Orbiter was lost Sept 23, 1999 (launched Dec 1998) when it entered Mars atmosphere on a too-low trajectory; (2) root cause was a units mismatch — Lockheed Martin ground software output thruster impulse in pound-force-seconds (US customary) while NASA's navigation software expected newton-seconds (SI), contrary to the Software Interface Specification. This is precisely a non-SI-to-SI conversion failure, matching the NIST supporting quote ('a subcontractor did not properly account for changing the non-SI measurements in its software'). (3) The $327.6 million figure matches NASA's stated total mission cost (orbiter+lander: $193.1M development + $91.7M launch + $42.8M ops). The quote supports the claim; no credible source disputes it. One minor nuance: $327.6M is the TOTAL Mars Surveyor '98 mission cost (orbiter + lander), not the orbiter alone — but the framing as 'a $327.6 million failure' is the standard NASA/NIST usage and is not misleading. This is the canonical textbook example for unit/dimensional-checking V&V, so its inclusion in the engineering verification skill is well-justified. input.caveats: 정확성 측면에서 명백히 틀린 항목은 발견되지 않았다. 주의해야 할 점: (1) ASME V&V/UQ는 본래 전산 모델(FEA/CFD/computational solid mechanics)용 표준이며, 제안한 7게이트 수계산(hand-calc) 하니스를 ASME가 직접 처방한 것이 아니다 — 원칙은 일반화되지만 구체적 게이트는 ASME에서 유도되지 않으므로 'ASME 준거'라고 과대표현하지 말 것. 수계산 desk-check는 ASME의 formal validation(실험 대비 비교)을 구성하지 않는다. (2) '식 선택 적합성' 게이트는 ASME validation보다 model-form 적합성/적용범위(domain of applicability) 개념에 더 정확히 매핑된다. (3) 치트시트 완전성 주의: Marin식은 6인자 전체 표기 권장, Se는 보정 내구한계여야 함(0.5Sut 아님), 오일러 좌굴은 탄성영역 한정(세장비 미만은 Johnson), 이론 K vs AISC 설계 권장 K 구분, K≈0.2는 큰 산포의 기본 가정값. (4) 출처 품질: 일부 공식은 2차 출처(LibreTexts, Wikipedia, engineersedge, pieng.com)에 의존하나 모두 표준 교과서(Shigley/Hibbeler/Norton)와 교차 확인되어 fundamentals 수준 주장에는 충분. (5) 연구 범위의 공백: 본 검증은 재료역학·기계요소·안전계수 중심으로 강하게 확인되었고, 열전달(푸리에/대류/복사), 유체(Darcy-Weisbach/Reynolds/Bernoulli), 기어·베어링 L10·용접·스프링 k, 산업별 안전계수 관례, order-of-magnitude 게이트, 재질 물성 범위에 대한 직접 1차 출처 확인은 25개 confirmed claim 안에 포함되지 않았다 — 이들 항목은 미검증 상태로 남아 있다.
